articles.title: Giá vàng hôm nay 11/10: SJC tăng 1,3 triệu/lượng, tín hiệu mới sau tuần biến động
articles.text:
Giá vàng thế giới hôm nay 11/10
Chỉ số tâm lý người tiêu dùng sơ bộ tháng 10 do Đại học Michigan (Mỹ) công bố giảm xuống 46,3 điểm, từ mức 48,1 điểm trong tháng 9. Kỳ vọng lạm phát trong một năm tới tăng lên 4,7%, còn kỳ vọng lạm phát dài hạn tăng lên 3,5%.
Báo cáo việc làm tháng 9 cho thấy Mỹ chỉ tạo thêm 29.000 việc làm. Tỷ lệ thất nghiệp duy trì ở mức 4,2%. Số liệu việc làm tháng 7 và tháng 8 được điều chỉnh giảm tổng cộng 60.000 việc làm.
Tâm lý tiêu dùng suy yếu làm gia tăng lo ngại về triển vọng tăng trưởng kinh tế Mỹ, qua đó hỗ trợ giá vàng. Tuy nhiên, kỳ vọng lạm phát tăng có thể khiến Fed tiếp tục duy trì chính sách lãi suất cao.
Thị trường đánh giá xác suất Fed tăng lãi suất trong tháng 10 vào khoảng 19%. Khả năng Fed tăng lãi suất ít nhất 0,25 điểm phần trăm trước tháng 12 lên tới 84%.
Lợi suất trái phiếu kho bạc Mỹ kỳ hạn 10 năm chốt phiên quanh 5,24%. Chỉ số USD duy trì gần 102,1 điểm.
Tình hình tại eo biển Hormuz và căng thẳng Mỹ - Iran tiếp tục tiềm ẩn rủi ro đối với nguồn cung năng lượng. Tuy nhiên, lo ngại về khả năng Mỹ tấn công Iran trong ngắn hạn đã giảm bớt.
Giá dầu Brent chốt phiên ở mức 104,72 USD/thùng, tăng 0,42%. Dầu WTI đạt 91,85 USD/thùng, tăng 0,39%.
Giá dầu cao, nguồn cung dầu diesel thắt chặt và rủi ro đối với tàu chở dầu làm gia tăng lo ngại lạm phát. Những yếu tố này có thể đẩy lợi suất trái phiếu lên, gây sức ép lên giá vàng. Tuy nhiên, căng thẳng địa chính trị vẫn hỗ trợ nhu cầu trú ẩn an toàn.
Chốt tuần, giá vàng giao ngay ở mức khoảng 4.195 USD/ounce. Giá vàng kỳ hạn tháng 11/2026 giao dịch quanh mức 4.220 USD/ounce.
Giá vàng trong nước hôm nay 11/10
Chốt phiên giao dịch ngày 10/10, giá vàng miếng SJC được niêm yết ở mức 141,8-144,8 triệu đồng/lượng (mua vào - bán ra), không thay đổi ở cả hai chiều so với chốt phiên giao dịch liền trước.
Giá vàng nhẫn loại 1-5 chỉ của SJC được niêm yết ở mức 141,3-144,3 triệu đồng/lượng (mua vào - bán ra), không thay đổi ở cả hai chiều so với chốt phiên giao dịch liền trước.
So với cuối tuần trước, giá vàng miếng SJC tăng 1,3 triệu đồng/lượng ở cả chiều mua vào và bán ra. Giá vàng nhẫn SJC loại 1-5 chỉ cũng tăng 1,3 triệu đồng/lượng ở cả hai chiều.
Giá vàng nhẫn trơn tại Bảo Tín Minh Châu được niêm yết ở mức 139,6-143,6 triệu đồng/lượng (mua vào - bán ra), giảm 300.000 đồng/lượng ở chiều mua vào và 200.000 đồng/lượng ở chiều bán ra so với chốt phiên giao dịch liền trước.
Dự báo giá vàng
Ông Darin Newsom, chuyên gia phân tích thị trường cấp cao tại Barchart, dự báo giá vàng tăng. Theo ông, các yếu tố nền tảng của thị trường chưa có nhiều thay đổi. Nếu Tổng thống Mỹ tiếp tục giữ quan điểm không tấn công Iran cho đến sau cuộc bầu cử giữa nhiệm kỳ, giá năng lượng có thể giảm, tạo điều kiện để kim loại quý phục hồi.
Xét về kỹ thuật, hợp đồng vàng giao tháng 12 đang ở vùng quá bán. Giá có thể phục hồi trong ngắn hạn. Tuy nhiên, giá vàng vẫn thấp hơn đáng kể so với đường trung bình động 45 ngày, hiện ở khoảng 4.398 USD/ounce.
Ông James Stanley, chiến lược gia thị trường cấp cao tại Forex, cho rằng lực bán có dấu hiệu suy yếu sau đợt giảm mạnh trong tuần. Việc giá vàng kết thúc tuần trong sắc xanh là tín hiệu đáng chú ý. Mốc 4.000 USD/ounce tiếp tục cho thấy lực mua xuất hiện khi giá lùi về vùng này.
Ông Adrian Day, Chủ tịch Adrian Day Asset Management, dự báo giá vàng chủ yếu dao động trong biên độ hẹp cho đến khi chiến sự kết thúc. Khi xung đột chấm dứt, kỳ vọng lạm phát giảm có thể làm giảm áp lực tăng lãi suất đối với các ngân hàng trung ương. Tuy nhiên, nhu cầu trú ẩn an toàn cũng có thể suy yếu.
Ông Day không kỳ vọng giá vàng giảm sâu nhưng cũng chưa cho rằng thị trường đủ điều kiện để bứt phá mạnh.

articles.title: What to expect from Apple’s ‘Welcome Home’ event
articles.text:
We are quickly coming up on Apple’s “Welcome Home” launch event, where we expect a host of smart home-related announcements. We are expecting refreshes to Apple TV and HomePod Mini, as well as a brand new smart home hub. We could also see the debut of a new platform called homeOS, and some partner devices from LG.
What to expect from Apple’s ‘Welcome Home’ event
Get ready for a smart home hub, a refreshed HomePod Mini, a faster Apple TV, and maybe some LG smart locks.
What we probably won’t be seeing is the long-rumored touchscreen MacBook, which Cupertino whisperer Mark Gurman says will debut later this month.
“Welcome Home” will officially kick off in New York on October 13th at 9AM ET. Here’s more about what to expect.
A proper smart home hub
Until now, Apple has primarily relied on the Home app to control all the various bits and bobs that make up your smart home. But it’s a market niche that the company has been eager to tackle more fully. The new device, which could be called HomePad or HomeView or, more simply, Apple Home Hub, will reportedly feature a 6-inch square touchscreen that can either be mounted on a wall or placed on a table or countertop. According to Mark Gurman, the countertop model will somewhat resemble the iMac G4, with the screen attached to an arm set into a half sphere.
Gurman seems to believe the device will be called HomeView, rather than HomePad. In part he believes that decision was driven by the fact that the hub will not be an iPad-like experience since there will be no App Store.
It will also supposedly use voice or facial recognition to identify who is interacting with it, pulling up the relevant contacts, calendar appointments, and more. Apple will offer the option for secondary identification through an iPhone to keep personal data more secure. The whole thing will reportedly run a new software platform called…
homeOS
The company may have registered a trademark for the name through a shell company called Home Operations Suite LLC, a move that Apple has pulled before to quietly secure the rights to names. The platform will supposedly feature a streamlined interface that “looks like a mashup of iOS, tvOS and watchOS,” according to Gurman. The focus, obviously, will be on smart home applications, like controlling thermostats and smart locks, and it will also be capable of making FaceTime calls.
The OS will also include your usual assortment of Apple apps and widgets, including Apple Music, Podcasts, and News, as well as Reminders, Notes, and Siri AI.
HomePod Mini and Apple TV get a minor refresh
Word is that not much is changing with the HomePod Mini or Apple TV. The designs will remain the same, but they’ll get a new processor to help handle the added demand of Siri AI. This will be the first update to the HomePod Mini since it was announced on October 13th of 2020 — exactly six years before Apple’s Welcome Home event. While the company isn’t making any dramatic changes for the Mini’s birthday, it will be offering it in new colors, including green and pink.
This will be the first hardware refresh for the Apple TV since 2022. In addition to supporting Siri AI, the new processor will also speed up navigation, which can get a bit laggy. Rumors are that it will have an integrated mic so that you won’t need to talk into the remote or a paired HomePod to control the Apple TV with Siri. The remote will also apparenlty have a speaker to make it easier to find.
Both are expected to feature Apple’s N1 chip, which includes support for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth 6.0.
LG and other partner devices
It’s likely that we’ll get a mention of products that integrate with HomeKit and offer new features built on top of homeOS and whatever Apple’s hardware hub ends up being called. But don’t expect Apple to share too much of the spotlight with its partners. We’ve already seen a leak of LG smart home, including deadbolts, thermostats, and more. They’ll also reportedly include an NFC-based “Proximity Control” that pops up a hint in the iPhone’s Dynamic Island when held near the device, as well as a “tap to set up without power” pairing feature.
Update October 11th, 2026: Added additional rumors from Mark Gurman’s Power On newsletter.

articles.title: Inside the Muslim Manosphere Policing Women Online
articles.text:
Mariam recently disabled Facebook Messenger. As the administrator of a Facebook group for women in the United Arab Emirates with close to 400,000 members, she’d become accustomed to receiving messages from strangers. But then came a shift in the volume—and nature—of those messages until they were impossible to ignore.
“Being the admin of this group has subjected me to all kinds of harassment,” says Miriam, who asked to be identified only by her first name because she fears online retaliation. They “either want to advise you to be holy and cover up, or they want to sexually harass you—or both.”
Mariam has run the group for more than a year. And even though intended for women, the group’s size and visibility has meant that Miriam also gets a lot of messages from men. She has received a deluge of unsolicited messages telling her how to dress, not to raise her voice or wear makeup, and to cover her hands with gloves so that no skin is visible.
“I couldn’t take it any longer. It was starting to affect my mental well-being,” Miriam says.
Many women who are conspicuous on the internet have been harassed online. That comes in countless forms, even if the same misogyny underlies it. The particular variety Miriam was subjected to stems from a section of the “manosphere” dressed in the clothes of religion—the Muslim manosphere.
At its core, the manosphere is built around male grievance and antifeminist ideology—though whether that’s entirely organic or engineered to sell supplements and other products is up for debate. Regardless, it has no shortage of subcultures to chose from: Incels, pick-up artists, men’s rights activists, and followers of the Red Pill.
Some nuances may make these groups distinct, but they largely share a common worldview: Feminism has destabilized society, women have acquired too much power, and men must reassert control. And the Muslim manosphere is no different. It’s adopted those ideas circulating through the wider manosphere and rebranded them in the language of faith.
Sarah Kaddoura, a feminist researcher and creator of the YouTube channel Haki Nasawi, examined the Arabic-speaking manosphere in a 2025 report. In her study, she describes some of the most prominent influencers, such as Jordanian relationship coach Kareem Atta’i, who posts online as Coach Kareem or Red Pill Arabic.
Atta’i packages his ideas as relationship advice, but his videos frequently frame interactions between men and women as contests for power. Atta’i’s videos, which WIRED Middle East has watched, describe violence as a means of “disciplining” women or retaliating against sexual rejection.
The Arabic manosphere does more than translate Western Red Pill content. Its creators have adapted the ideology to local anxieties around religion, masculinity, marriage, money, and social change.
Kaddoura says influencers use financial insecurity, political instability, religious identity, and fears about declining morality or social cohesion to build their audiences. Misogyny becomes an explanation for a much wider sense of frustration—and women become its most visible target.
The problem is not religious expression online but the use of religious authority—real or claimed—to legitimize misogyny, harassment, and the public surveillance of women. The Muslim manosphere is also not confined to the Arab world. Like the broader manosphere, it crosses borders, languages, and platforms.
Take prominent UK-based creator Ali Dawah, whose channel features street debates and commentary about relationships, gender roles, religion, and Western culture. In one clip, Dawah says he hates Muslim feminists “the most.” In another video, he approaches women in public and challenges them over clothing he describes as immodest.
“Dawah” is not just this YouTuber’s name. In Arabic, it means to make an invitation to someone to learn about Islam. Ali is just one of many influencers often called “Dawah Bros,” and they’re generally known for being more aggressive than offering an invitation when it comes to promoting their manosphere-esque content.
Kaddoura sees the Dawah Bros as a platform-native successor to an older variety of media figure. During the 1990s, Islamic television programs in Egypt and Saudi Arabia regularly featured sheikhs answering callers’ questions about relationships, clothing, and acceptable behavior. However, unlike television preachers, today’s influencers are not limited to scheduled broadcasts, and they aren’t only interacting with people who’ve chosen to call in.
For many Muslim women—especially those who are in prominent places on the internet—these ideas do not remain confined to podcasts or debate videos. They spill into comment sections and private messages, where strangers appoint themselves enforcers of morality.
A 2026 report by the Institute for Strategic Dialogue analyzed nearly 14,000 comments directed at 40 prominent public figures and influencers on Instagram in Jordan over a 12-month period. Among comments classified as hate speech, harassment, or abusive language, 72 percent targeted women, 11 percent were classified as religious or moral harassment, and the vast majority of those comments—85 percent—targeted female influencers.
Additionally, all of the comments classified as sexual harassment were directed at women, underlining the pervasive contradictions in how women are policed on the internet—the same online environment that instructing women to make themselves invisible also subjecting them to unwanted sexual attention. That contradiction is visible in the messages Mariam has received.
The manosphere’s reach is shaped in part by the recommendation systems that determine what users encounter in their feeds. “As soon as you create an account on TikTok, YouTube, X, Instagram, and others as a male, it doesn’t take long for the algorithm to start recommending misogynistic content,” Kaddoura says.
Engagement-based systems can amplify emotionally charged and polarizing content, including manosphere videos. Content blaming women for men’s loneliness or financial insecurity can generate reactions from supporters, critics, and the women being targeted. Those interactions may increase its visibility.
That becomes even thornier when religion enters the picture. The relationship coaches and other men preaching religion online often present personal opinions as religious instruction, Kaddoura says. This can make disagreement appear immoral, and criticism can then be presented as evidence that the creator is defending the faith against hostile forces.
But how exactly a user’s behavior tips over from passively encountering the content to actively engaging with it remains an open question. Researchers can examine publicly available videos and identify influential accounts, but they have limited access to the internal data needed to trace how users move between creators and communities. This leave key questions unanswered, such as whether prolonged exposure changes their behavior.
For women such as Mariam, the technical route behind the harassment may be invisible, but its effects are not. A creator publishes a video. Recommendation systems carry it into other users’ feeds. And then, eventually, users repeat its message in women’s comment sections and inboxes. Repeat ad infinitum.
WIRED Middle East contacted Ali Dawah and Kareem Atta’i for comment. Neither responded by the time of publication.
This story originally appeared in WIRED Middle East.

articles.title: Giá rau củ tăng mạnh; lợn hơi trong nước giảm giá sâu
articles.text:
Giá rau củ tăng mạnh, một loại rau gia vị đắt ngang 1kg thịt heo
Giá rau củ tại TPHCM tiếp tục tăng cao, trong đó một số loại rau gia vị đã vượt 100.000 đồng/kg. Tiểu thương cho biết có loại rau hiện có giá ngang một số loại thịt heo bán tại chợ.
Đơn cử, giá rau cải bó xôi tại chợ dao động từ 70.000 đồng/kg, cải ngọt, cải xanh từ 55.000-60.000 đồng/kg, tăng khoảng 20.000 đồng so với ngày thường; rau xà lách từ 45.000-55.000 đồng/kg, tăng 5.000-10.000 đồng/kg.
Nhóm rau gia vị như rau ngò rí 10.000-12.000 đồng/lạng, tức 100.000-120.000 đồng/kg tùy điểm bán, hành lá 80.000-90.000 đồng/kg. Nhóm có mức giá ít tăng hoặc giữ nguyên như cà rốt, su hào, bí đao, bí đỏ, bắp cải tròn Đà Lạt cỡ nhỏ dao động từ 15.000-35.000 đồng/kg tùy loại.
Bà Thảo, tiểu thương tại chợ Phạm Văn Bạch, xác nhận giá rau về chợ duy trì ở mức cao do ảnh hưởng của thời tiết và một phần do giá nhiên liệu. Hiện rau ăn lá và rau gia vị là nhóm mặt hàng tăng giá mạnh nhất do dễ bị dập và hư hỏng khi gặp mưa.
Chi gần 2,2 tỷ USD nhập khẩu thịt; lợn hơi trong nước giảm giá sâu
Tính đến hết tháng 9 năm nay, nước ta đã chi ra gần 2,2 tỷ USD để nhập khẩu thịt và các sản phẩm từ thịt. Theo đó, các loại thịt gia cầm, thịt lợn và thịt trâu giá rẻ tiếp tục tràn về Việt Nam.
Giá của những loại thịt nhập khẩu này được rao bán rẻ hơn khoảng 20-50% so với các mặt hàng nội địa cùng phân khúc.
Giá trung bình nhập khẩu thịt heo tươi ướp lạnh hoặc đông lạnh về Việt Nam trong 8 tháng đầu năm 2026 ở mức 1.712 USD/tấn, giảm 36% so với cùng kỳ.
Tính bình quân, giá nhập khẩu thịt heo về Việt Nam chỉ khoảng 45.000 đồng/kg. Mức giá này chưa bằng một nửa giá thịt heo tại các chợ truyền thống ở TPHCM, nơi giá bán bình quân từ 100.000 đồng/kg.
Đáng chú ý, giá lợn hơi xuất chuồng đã giảm xuống mức thấp nhất trong năm. Trong khi dự báo giá lợn hơi trong ngắn hạn sẽ tiếp tục xu hướng giảm nhẹ hoặc đi ngang.
Cập nhật đến 5/10, giá lợn hơi tại khu vực miền Bắc và miền Nam dao động từ 54.000-56.000 đồng/kg; miền Trung ở mức 55.000-56.000 đồng/kg.
Thịt heo nhập khẩu giá rẻ chưa dễ thay thế thịt tươi trong bữa cơm người Việt, nhưng đang tìm được đầu ra ở bếp ăn công nghiệp và các sản phẩm chế biến.
Mỹ tăng mua một loại hạt của Việt Nam, giảm nhập từ Ấn Độ và Indonesia
Thống kê của Cục Hải quan cho thấy, trong tháng 9/2026, Việt Nam xuất khẩu 25.152 tấn hạt tiêu, thu về gần 164 triệu USD, tăng 10,6% về lượng và 10,8% về giá trị so với tháng trước.
Lũy kế đến hết tháng 9 năm nay, nước ta đã xuất bán gần 217.000 tấn hạt được ví như “vàng đen”, kim ngạch đạt 1,41 tỷ USD. So với cùng kỳ năm ngoái, xuất khẩu hạt tiêu tăng 16,2% về khối lượng và tăng 11,4% về giá trị.
Đáng chú ý, thị phần hạt tiêu Việt Nam trong tổng lượng nhập khẩu của Mỹ tăng lên 80,4%, củng cố vị thế nguồn cung lớn nhất tại thị trường này.
Trung Quốc gom mua hàng triệu tấn gạo của Việt Nam, chỉ sau một quốc gia
Theo báo cáo mới nhất của Bộ Nông nghiệp và Môi trường, trong tháng 9, nước ta xuất khẩu 377.400 tấn gạo, thu về 205,6 triệu USD.
Lũy kế 9 tháng năm 2026, các doanh nghiệp nước ta xuất khẩu khoảng 6,4 triệu tấn gạo, trị giá 3,11 tỷ USD. So với cùng kỳ năm ngoái, xuất khẩu gạo giảm 6,1% về khối lượng và giảm 10,9% về giá trị.
Trong 8 tháng năm 2026, Trung Quốc chi gần 505 triệu USD nhập khẩu hơn 1 triệu tấn gạo Việt Nam, vươn lên vị trí thị trường xuất khẩu lớn thứ hai của gạo Việt, sau Philippines.
Giá xăng E10 tăng hơn 1.000 đồng/lít, dầu diesel giảm
Giá xăng dầu tại kỳ điều hành 8/10 được điều chỉnh theo hướng xăng và dầu mazut được điều chỉnh tăng, trong khi giá dầu diesel giảm. Theo đó, giá xăng E10 tăng hơn 1.000 đồng/lít, trong khi giá dầu diesel giảm gần 600 đồng/lít.
Liên quan đến xăng dầu, tại họp báo thường kỳ chiều 7/10, đại diện Bộ Công Thương chia sẻ rõ hơn về đề xuất để doanh nghiệp tự quyết định giá xăng dầu, đồng thời cho rằng khó xảy ra tình trạng thương nhân đầu mối có thể chi phối hoàn toàn giá bán trên thị trường.
iPhone 18 vừa mở bán đã có máy kích hoạt, rẻ hơn tới 3,5 triệu đồng
Các mẫu iPhone 18 vừa ra mắt đã bắt đầu xuất hiện tại một số hệ thống bán lẻ dưới dạng máy đã kích hoạt. Theo khảo sát, iPhone 18 Pro 512GB đã kích hoạt được bán với giá 41,99 triệu đồng, thấp hơn 3,5 triệu đồng so với mức 45,49 triệu đồng của máy mới cùng dung lượng.
Với bản 256GB, giá máy đã kích hoạt khoảng 36,49 triệu đồng, thấp hơn 2,5 triệu đồng so với máy mới, hiện được niêm yết ở mức 38,99 triệu đồng.
Trong khi đó, iPhone 18 Pro Max 256GB đã kích hoạt có giá khoảng 41,99 triệu đồng, tương đương máy mới cùng dung lượng.

articles.title: US probes Foxconn, Luxshare over AI server power patents
articles.text:
AUS trade body has opened a patent case against 20 companies over the power systems inside AI servers. Foxconn, Luxshare and Quanta are among them.The US International Trade Commission acted after a complaint by power-chip maker Vicor, it said on Friday. Vicor says their products infringe one of its patents.
Twenty names on the list
The case covers systems that feed power to top-end chips from directly below them, and the computers that use them.
Besides Foxconn, Luxshare and Quanta, the companies named include Delta Electronics, Monolithic Power Systems, Infineon, Flex and Celestica.
Vicor wants the products barred from the US, and the firms ordered to stop selling them.
Luxshare plays it down
Apple supplier Luxshare said in a filing on Saturday that it does not expect the probe to have a material impact on its production, operations or results, Bloomberg reported.
The products are still being tested by customers and are not in mass production, Luxshare said. The commission has not ruled on the claims yet.
The commission will set a target date to finish the case within 45 days. Any import ban could only take effect after a full hearing and a final ruling.
Luxshare listed in Hong Kong in July, in the city’s biggest IPO this year.

articles.title: These Midterm Races Will Decide Data Centers’ Political Fate
articles.text:
Welcome back to Power Play! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Molly an email at [email protected] or reach them securely on Signal at mollytaft.76.
From surveillance and DOGE to Big Tech money and religious extremism, the midterms have never been more WIRED. Data centers are no exception: The public has rapidly turned on them since the beginning of the year.
The opposition is bipartisan, with many Republicans making a rare break from President Donald Trump. Candidates on both sides of the aisle are trying to attack their opponents for being pro–data center (or not anti–data center enough). I’ve spotted at least five candidates who have been given the derogatory “Data Center [Name]” moniker by their opponents, in an attempt to highlight their connections to the industry. (That includes two guys named Derek/Derrick getting this treatment.)
While polling shows that pocketbook issues are likely to be top of voters’ minds, data centers are a potent-enough issue that they could swing tight races—and ultimately tip the balance of power in Congress. Here are some of the races WIRED is keeping an eye on as we approach November 3.
The National Republican Senatorial Committee issued a memo in August warning that Democrat Sherrod Brown, running for Senate in Ohio, was hitting his opponent, Senator Jon Husted, so hard on data centers that it could tip the outcome of the race, calling it “a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle.” Brown has called Husted “the face of data centers in Ohio,” running ads that blame Husted for welcoming data centers to the state and driving energy bills up.
Senate Democrats have taken up Brown’s cause, torpedoing a bill sponsored by Husted and modeled after the White House’s ratepayer protection pledge, with Minority Leader Chuck Schumer calling the bill “toothless.”
Data centers have also seeped into many other toss-up Senate races, including in Michigan, Iowa, and Texas. But the Ohio race is still the top one to watch here.
All 435 seats in the House are up for grabs, and data centers have become flash points in dozens of races across the country. Among races labeled toss-ups by the Cook Political Report, I found numerous examples of candidates running data-center-related ads:
- In Michigan’s 7th district, Will Lawrence used local opposition to data centers to help win a tough Democratic primary. Lawrence is now facing off against Republican Tom Barrett and has aired several data-center-related ads, both attacking Barrett and advertising Lawrence’s promise to “stand up to corporate power.”
- In Pennsylvania’s 8th district, Republican incumbent Rob Bresnahan has run ads promising to be tough on the industry—despite holding data-center-related stocks and a previously friendly stance. His Democratic challenger, Paige Cognetti, has also run ads attacking the industry.
- In Ohio’s 9th, Democratic incumbent Marcy Kaptur has run ads railing against what she says is incumbent Derek Merrin’s history of giving tax breaks to data centers. (The ads call him “Data Center Derek.”) Merrin claims that Kaptur is misrepresenting his vote on a broader bill.
- In Wisconsin’s 3rd district, Democrat Rebecca Cooke has aired attack ads against incumbent Derrick van Orden’s history of taking contributions from data center developers, dubbing him “DC Derrick.” (Sound familiar?) Van Orden has also shot back by highlighting Cooke’s ties to the tech industry, claiming she is “responsible for covering up pristine Wisconsin farmland” with data centers.
- In New York’s 17th district, incumbent Republican Mike Lawler has aired an ad slamming Democratic opponent Cait Conley’s past statements that the Hudson Valley “needs” data centers.
At least 20 candidates in the 36 gubernatorial races have promised to enact some kind of data center moratorium if elected, according to research from Multistate. The only true hyperscale moratorium in place in the US right now was signed in July by New York governor Kathy Hochul, who holds a comfortable lead ahead of challenger Bruce Blakeman (who supports data center development).
Candidates without much daylight between them have still tried to gain the upper hand on the issue. In Wisconsin’s tight gubernatorial race, Republican Tom Tiffany has attacked Democrat David Crowley with ads calling him “Data Center David.” Both candidates say they support restrictions on the industry.
In states that have been hotbeds for data center activity, some candidates in tight races have been forced to pivot on the issue. Nowhere is this clearer than in Texas, where incumbent governor Greg Abbott has gone from welcoming data center development to putting a de facto moratorium on permits in less than a year. His opponent, Gina Hinojosa, says Abbott hasn’t gone far enough to regulate the industry.
Voters in eight states are looking at more than 30 local ballot measures around data centers. Once again, Ohio is a standout here: It’s responsible for more than half of those measures, from local moratoriums to referendums around rezoning.
What We’re Writing
WIRED science editor Brian Kahn and I got exclusive access to a startup that wants to pull water from the air using excess heat from data centers. While atmospheric water-harvesting technology has been around for a while, the startup has a unique spin. Atoco uses materials known as metal organic frameworks, or MOFs, which won one of its founders the Nobel Prize last year. The company’s previous prototypes have all needed to be hooked up to the grid to generate enough heat to extract water from the MOFs. The new version, though, only needs waste heat from industrial facilities—like data centers—to produce water, even in arid areas.
What We’re Reading
- In Memphis, Tennessee, home of Elon Musk’s SpaceX data centers, the city council postponed a vote on a data center moratorium. Business Insider has more on the “chaotic” meeting.
- Bloomberg reports that Oracle used trucks to ship in natural gas to a data center outside Salt Lake City to keep it online for more than a year—and is considering a similar move in New Mexico, where pipeline delays have held up a big project.
- As the midterms approach, environmental groups are flooding the zone with ads about the rush to build AI infrastructure powered by fossil fuels—just as Congress prepares to debate permitting reform. Heatmap has more.

articles.title: Horror is big business
articles.text:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on how pervasive horror has become, follow Andrew Webster. The Stepback, arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.
Horror is big business
The genre has become a tentpole across gaming, film, and television.
Horror is big business
The genre has become a tentpole across gaming, film, and television.
How it started
Resident Evil has been around for 30 years, but the survival horror series is more popular than ever. The most recent game, Resident Evil Requiem, has sold 8 million copies since it launched in February, already making it the 14th best-selling game that Capcom has ever made. At the same time, a reboot of the Resident Evil film series from Weapons director Zach Cregger is on pace to become the top-grossing movie in franchise history. This has had the effect of renewing interest in Resident Evil at large; according to a report from Game File, six different titles in the game series have sold at least 3 million copies so far this year. In an earnings report, Capcom called it “a virtuous cycle in which sales of both new and past titles grow together.”
Resident Evil isn’t alone. Rather, it’s indicative of an ongoing trend. Horror was once seen as largely a niche genre, but now, thanks to a combination of factors — including the rise of YouTube and widespread influence of indie games and viral memes — it has steadily grown into a dominant force. Horror tends to be cheaper to produce than other genres, but now it also has sales numbers that compete with the biggest blockbusters. It’s not that there haven’t been major horror success stories before. 2017’s It remains the top-grossing horror flick of all time, and the Resident Evil 2 remake from 2019 has sold almost 20 million copies. But in 2026 the concentration of horror hits, particularly across multiple mediums, has reached a new level, making it clearer than ever that scaring audiences is a big business.
How it’s going
The most obvious example of this in 2026 is in movies. Obsession and Backrooms — two films helmed by young directors who came up through YouTube — have raked in nearly $1 billion combined at the box office. They out-grossed established franchises like Star Wars and even legendary directors like Steven Spielberg. This despite costing a fraction of what a blockbuster film usually costs; Backrooms was made for an estimated $10 million, while Obsession cost less than $1 million. Before that, Iron Lung, another YouTube-centric horror flick, managed to rake in more than $50 million without the backing of a major studio. Horror movies have always been comparatively cheap to make, but now they’re frequently able to make a huge return on that investment.
Meanwhile, in the world of streaming, October has become something of a battleground. This year basically every major service has a tentpole series meant to lure subscribers during spooky season. Amazon just released a remake of Stephen King’s Carrie on Prime Video, helmed by Mike Flanagan, who made his name with a quintet of limited horror series on Netflix between 2018 and 2023, starting with The Haunting of Hill House. With Flanagan now at Amazon, Netflix’s big release this year is Below, a six-episode sea monster thriller starring Josh Hartnett and Stranger Things’ Charlie Heaton. Elsewhere, Peacock has a Friday the 13th prequel called Crystal Lake starring Linda Cardellini as Jason Voorhees’ mom, and AMC Plus is putting out a spooky detective series called Yaga, which features Carrie-Anne Moss and Heated Rivalry’s Hudson Williams. Not to be excluded, Disney Plus is currently airing the 13th season of American Horror Story.
The one name missing from this list is Apple TV, but that’s because the service got a jump on things by releasing the horror / comedy hybrid Widow’s Bay back in April. The show then proceeded to win a record number of Emmys, and it remains a fixture on Apple TV’s most-watched list. While streaming viewership data is much harder to come by than box office data, the sheer fact that every major streaming service is investing in horror-related series, with the backing of some major star power, is an indication of just how important it is.
And then there are games. While Resident Evil is the biggest name, there are plenty of other titles and franchises that have been buoyed by the current horror renaissance. Silent Hill has been on a steady run, highlighted by the Scottish spinoff Townfall this year, and the iconic Hellraiser just got its first proper video game adaptation. But it’s not just blockbuster releases. Indie horror games have not only been consistent bestsellers on platforms like Steam, they’ve also been the source material for a number of more moderate theatrical hits, including both Iron Lung and Exit 8. And a lot of that success begins with people watching horror games on Twitch and YouTube; Twitch says that viewers watched 287 million hours of horror content between January and September this year, and that the dedicated “horror” tag saw a 6 percent increase in viewership compared to last year.
What happens next
With the potential to make a lot of money with very little investment, movie studios are naturally jumping all over the trend. Kane Parsons has reportedly signed up for a Backrooms sequel, Obsession director Curry Barker already has a new film due out next year, and Cregger’s next film has some major star power behind it. Meanwhile, studios are searching for the next Backrooms or Five Nights at Freddy’s anywhere they can. Both A24 and Neon are working on competing movies set in the SCP Foundation universe, a sort of terrifying and expansive fan-made project about a mysterious organization that keeps supernatural and paranormal entities secret, while Warner Bros. has scooped up the rights to internet phenomenon Siren Head. Elsewhere, both Silent Hill and Resident Evil have settled on a near-annual release schedule that shows no signs of slowing down — Capcom says that the ongoing success of Resident Evil led to a new quarterly sales record — nor does the horror fixation of major streaming services. Amazon went so far as to poach Flanagan from Netflix with an exclusive deal, and a struggling Xbox has invested in bringing Hideo Kojima’s horror game OD to consoles.
Obviously not all of these projects will be major hits. Not every spooky meme will become a Backrooms-level success. But studios, streamers, and game publishers are taking the genre more seriously now because that potential exists, and they seem more willing to take risks because the upfront costs aren’t as high. This means that, unlike other genres, the possibility remains that even as it explodes in popularity, horror will continue to remain weird and unexpected. After all, the best way to scare folks is to show them something new.
By the way
- Success in one medium doesn’t necessarily translate. While Silent Hill has become a force in games again, the most recent film has been largely forgotten.
- The SCP Foundation has garnered plenty of interest from major film studios, but not without some controversy due to its Creative Commons roots.
- Box office success aside, 2026 has also just been a really great year for horror movies with the likes of Send Help, Hokum, and 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple.
- Another potential venue for horror: interactive shows. Netflix is exploring the space with Unhinged and an upcoming Conjuring spinoff.
Read this
- The new iteration of Carrie makes some major changes, and in an interview with Collider Flanagan explains what went into updating the story.
- The New Yorker has a great rundown on just how YouTube became the place where new horror auteurs are discovered.
- 2026 has made it clear just how closely horror and comedy are related, and few people know that more than Jordan Peele, who discussed it in an old interview with The Guardian.

articles.title: Giá xăng dầu hôm nay 11/10: Thế giới trải qua tuần tăng, trong nước trái chiều
articles.text:
Giá dầu thế giới hôm nay
Giá dầu quốc tế trong tuần này trải qua một tuần đầy biến động với 3 phiên tăng và 2 phiên giảm.
Cụ thể, trong phiên giao dịch đầu tuần này (5/10), giá dầu thế giới giảm gần 2%, trong bối cảnh khối lượng xuất khẩu dầu thô của Trung Đông tăng trở lại và Nhóm các nước công nghiệp phát triển hàng đầu thế giới (G7) quyết định xả kho dự trữ.
Ngày 2/10, các nước G7 nhất trí giải phóng 100 triệu thùng dầu thô và dầu diesel từ các kho dự trữ khẩn cấp, đồng thời cam kết không áp đặt các biện pháp hạn chế xuất khẩu năng lượng sau sức ép từ Tổng thống Mỹ Donald Trump.
Giá dầu thế giới nhích tăng nhẹ trong phiên giao dịch 6/10, khi thị trường cân nhắc sự phục hồi của dòng dầu thô xuất khẩu từ Trung Đông cùng kế hoạch xả kho dự trữ khẩn cấp của Nhóm G7. Các yếu tố này đã làm giảm bớt những lo ngại về nguồn cung.
Đến phiên giao dịch 7/10, giá dầu thế giới giảm nhẹ sau khi Cơ quan Thông tin Năng lượng Mỹ (EIA) nhất trí đẩy nhanh việc giải phóng dầu từ kho dự trữ chiến lược, đồng thời ưu tiên nguồn dầu diesel, nhằm góp phần hạ nhiệt giá nhiên liệu đang ở mức cao.
Tuy nhiên, tới phiên giao dịch 8/10, giá dầu thế giới đảo chiều tăng hơn 4% trong bối cảnh tình hình Trung Đông tiếp tục diễn biến phức tạp, làm gia tăng lo ngại về nguy cơ gián đoạn nguồn cung, trong khi hoạt động khai thác dầu tại vịnh Mexico của Mỹ bị ảnh hưởng bởi bão Isaias.
Ở phiên giao dịch cuối cùng của tuần này (9/10), giá dầu thế giới tăng nhẹ khi cơn bão Isaias tiến về phía bờ biển phía Bắc vịnh Mexico của Mỹ, khiến hàng loạt cơ sở khai thác ngoài khơi phải tạm ngừng hoạt động. Diễn biến này làm dấy lên lo ngại về nguy cơ gián đoạn nguồn cung năng lượng toàn cầu.
Tính chung trong cả tuần này, giá dầu Brent tăng 2,4 USD/thùng, trong khi giá dầu WTI tăng 0,74 USD/thùng.
Giá dầu Brent đóng cửa tuần này ở mức 104,7 USD/thùng, còn giá dầu WTI kết tuần ở mức 91,85 USD/thùng.
Giá xăng dầu trong nước hôm nay
Ở thị trường trong nước, giá bán các mặt hàng xăng dầu tuần này được điều chỉnh theo hướng xăng tăng, dầu diesel giảm gần 600 đồng/lít.
Cụ thể, ở kỳ điều hành 8/10, giá xăng E5RON92 tăng 1.134 đồng/lít, giá bán không cao hơn 27.703 đồng/lít.
Tương tự, giá xăng E10RON95-III được điều chỉnh tăng 1.065 đồng/lít, giá bán lẻ không cao hơn 28.254 đồng/lít.
Trái lại, giá dầu diesel 0.05S giảm 589 đồng/lít, xuống mức không cao hơn 29.128 đồng/lít.
Trong khi giá dầu mazut 180CST 3.5S được điều chỉnh tăng 701 đồng/kg, lên mức không cao hơn 21.092 đồng/kg.
Dữ liệu từ Bộ Công Thương cho thấy, giá bán lẻ xăng dầu tại Việt Nam hiện ở mức thấp hơn so với các nước có chung đường biên giới.
Liên bộ Công Thương - Tài chính đang tiếp tục theo dõi sát diễn biến thị trường để thông báo giá xăng dầu phù hợp với diễn biến thị trường và kịp thời đề xuất Chính phủ, Thủ tướng các giải pháp bình ổn giá xăng dầu.

articles.title: Let’s Talk About the Super El Niño and Climate Change
articles.text:
The tropical Pacific has seen heat build for months as a “super” El Niño takes shape.
A climate phenomenon that forms every few years, this year’s iteration of El Niño has been on a tear of daily records and is forecast to reach unprecedented strength this winter. While it’s characterized by hotter-than-normal waters in the eastern tropical Pacific, El Niño is a global problem.
It’s fair to wonder how another global problem is interacting with El Niño: climate change, driven by burning fossil fuels. While a hotter climate begetting a hotter El Niño might seem like a done deal, “I have more questions than I have reactions” to what’s happening, says Christopher Callahan, a climate researcher at Indiana University. In other words, the relationship is still an area of active research—and this year’s event could provide vital insights.
El Niño’s added ocean heat affects the atmosphere, causing weather patterns around the world to shift. Consider it kind of like a domino run, where one tile starts a chain reaction. Such a major slug of heat in the Pacific will act more like a shove then a light flick on the atmosphere, and the resulting shifts in weather are expected to be generationally intense.
The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is forecasting 100 percent odds of an extremely strong El Niño through December and above 80 percent odds it stays that way through February. Data shows this El Niño has already set multiple all-time daily heat records including a recent peak of 3.4 degrees Celsius.
NOAA issues its El Niño forecast as a three-month rolling average, and the agency predicts heat could peak at 2.7 degrees Celsius above normal for the period from October to December. (It’s not out of the question that heat could surpass 3 degrees Celsius, though.) If the forecast holds true, it would smash the previous record of 2.4 degrees Celsius, which was set during the 1982-1983 event.
How Is Climate Change Impacting El Niño?
There is a growing body of evidence that climate change is likely playing at least some role in influencing El Niño. The magnitude and frequency of the phenomenon has increased over the past 60 years, says Francisco Estrada, coordinator of the Climate Change Research Program at the National Autonomous University of Mexico, and so has the variability and how the effects are distributed around the world. He says there shouldn’t be a debate framed as a choice between a “natural El Niño” and an “El Niño caused by climate change” but rather as an interaction between the two processes.
“You can’t separate El Niño from global warming—they’re inextricably linked,” he explains.
Modeling also indicates that El Niño is likely to strengthen as the planet warms, though Callahan notes that many models struggle to accurately represent long-term temperature trends in the eastern tropical Pacific. That can give researchers some pause, but there’s also other evidence that climate change is juicing El Niño.
“The majority of climate models say that El Nino amplitude shall go up in a warming climate, and all of our paleoclimate records say that we're currently in a more active period of El Niño than the last several 1,000 years,” Callahan says.
Research published in August uses data collected from ancient coral, and provides that 1,000-year glimpse Callahan mentions. (He wasn’t involved with the study.) The scientists found an uptick in El Niño amplitude that neatly mirrors when humans started pumping greenhouse gases into the atmosphere, though they didn’t attempt to attribute the shift to climate change.
This year’s El Niño will provide another data point to help researchers suss things out.
How Is El Niño Impacting Climate Change?
But as Callahan notes, there’s also an important question about how El Niño is layering on top of climate change.
“Even if climate change has not made the event itself stronger, even if the [sea surface temperature] anomalies are totally natural, the presence of those SSTs in a climate that has been changed by global warming might produce unprecedented impacts,” he says.
El Niño’s impacts on weather—known as teleconnections—are well known, from increasing the odds of drought in the Amazon and Indonesia to juicing precipitation in the Southwest US and lowering the odds of Atlantic hurricanes.
Such an extreme event layered on top of climate change doesn’t mean teleconnections get thrown out the window, though. In fact, some of them may be even more intense.
“We can no longer place as much confidence in the knowledge we’ve gathered from data regarding how El Niño manifests in terms of weather and climate in different parts of the planet,” says Estrada.
What El Niño Means for Climate Risk
From a risk perspective, Estrada believes it’s important to understand how the two phenomena interact and how that combination will affect societies.
He and Callahan’s main concern is not merely whether this El Niño will be the most intense on record but rather the combination of an exceptional event with a climate that has warmed significantly.
“Surprises are the last thing you want when you’re trying to manage risk,” Estrada says.
Callahan’s work shows that the impacts of El Niño on society are extreme, with the most severe events knocking off trillions of dollars from the global GDP. Ecosystems also suffer greatly, particularly coral reefs, which are facing a mass bleaching event.
Given this scenario, the United Nations and other international organizations have called for urgent adaptation measures to safeguard the well-being of the at-risk populations and ecosystems. Some places are already doing that: California preemptively declared a state of emergency last month.
“El Niño conditions will pour fuel on the fire of a warming world. Impacts will hit even harder, travel even farther, and cross borders with devastating speed,” UN Secretary-General António Guterres said last month.
Additional reporting by Brian Kahn.

articles.title: Parents near Tesla’s Fremont plant question emissions plan
articles.text:
Parents at an elementary school next to Tesla’s Fremont car plant want more time to question a plan that could raise emissions from the factory, Matthew Brown reported for SFGate.
Lila Bringhurst Elementary sits less than 1,000 feet from the plant. Tesla has applied to change emission limits on two aluminium melting furnaces and add new equipment to cut nitrogen oxides, according to a notice from the Bay Area Air District.
“It was sort of obfuscating”
The notice reached parents in a single school app message on 3 September. It said limits would be modified, but not that they could go up, parents said.
“It was sort of obfuscating,” parent Jenny Lin told SFGate.
Many only took notice after an anonymous Substack post on 1 October. Using the district’s own engineering papers, it claimed one measure of emissions would rise thirteenfold. Parts of the review were blacked out, including limits the district would place on Tesla.
The district told SFGate it must redact trade secrets, and would check the documents for errors.
Not all dust is equal
The thirteenfold figure covers all suspended particles, including harmless ones. Much of that is larger dust that does not enter the body, said Nicholas Spada, an air quality researcher at UC Davis.
He still called the jump “significant”.
The district says the estimates stay within its limits, and it would require continuous monitoring on the furnaces.
A petition asking it to extend the comment period, which ended on Monday, passed 1,000 signatures. The plant is already under investigation by the district over allegedly inaccurate emissions reports.
Tesla did not respond to SFGate’s request for comment.

articles.title: AI won’t fix America’s debt, Guardian analysis argues
articles.text:
The White House hopes AI will help the US grow its way out of debt. That is a new take on the Reagan-era promise that tax cuts pay for themselves, Eduardo Porter argued in an analysis for The Guardian.
“Even if AI supercharged the economy, its impact on the government’s finances would be muted,” he wrote.
Growth the US has rarely seen
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is relying on AI to help deliver 3% annual growth, a rate the US has rarely hit this century, Porter wrote.
The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a fiscal watchdog, has run the numbers. To cut the deficit to 3% of GDP by 2036, the economy would need to grow about 4.4% a year. Balancing the budget would take about 7.2%.
The group’s own estimates of AI’s boost to growth are far smaller. The Congressional Budget Office expects AI to add about 0.1 percentage points a year.
Winners don’t pay as much tax
Porter argues that AI would shift income from workers to the owners of capital. In the US, capital is taxed at about half the rate of labour, so the government would collect less from the same growth.
The AI boom also competes with the government for investors’ money. Tech giants are borrowing heavily to build data centres, as US debt passed 100% of GDP.
The payback problem
Big Tech also needs AI to pay off. Economists Jared Bernstein and Ryan Cummings estimate the largest cloud firms need $13.1tn to $18.7tn in extra revenue over a decade to justify their spending.
If those targets are missed, Porter wrote, it could make the US debt even harder to finance.

articles.title: California’s Tallest and Most Iconic Trees Are Getting Heatstroke
articles.text:
This story originally appeared on Vox and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
A grove of coast redwood trees is a forest of forests. Individual trees can live for thousands of years, and as they grow, their canopies develop mats of soils and ferns, creating something like a second forest floor hundreds of feet above the ground.
These elevated ecosystems are home to creatures like the wandering salamander, which can spend its entire life cycle on top of a single tree, and the marbled murrelet, a seabird whose nesting habits were a mystery until one day in 1974, when a tree-trimmer stumbled upon a nest 150 feet above the ground. Sometimes a stray seed—a sitka spruce or oak or even another redwood—finds its way up a massive redwood and grows into another tree entirely, nestled among the branches of a giant.
For millennia, redwoods have been the anchors of this incredibly stable ecosystem; they can even survive wildfires that devastate other tree species. They’ve also been the source of plenty of human inspiration and drive millions of dollars to California’s tourist economy. But like other living things, they aren’t immune to warming temperatures, and it turns out these trees have a particular weak spot.
A new study from researchers at the University of California, Davis, using measurements taken twice a month for two years, found that coast redwood leaves essentially dial down their photosynthesis during periods of extreme heat. This means trees are slowing their “breathing” and “eating” because they can’t cool down fast enough when temperatures rise. It’s a problem that’s only going to get worse as climate change continues to drive global temperatures up, and it raises urgent questions about the future of these iconic trees and the layers of life that live on and around their shadow-dappled lengths.
To understand what’s happening to the redwoods—and what that may mean for the species that rely on them—first we need to take a quick foray into tree anatomy. Trees use the pores in their leaves, stomata, to do two things: take carbon dioxide in, and let water out. Open stomata mean the tree is “breathing” in carbon dioxide and photosynthesizing, but probably also letting water out. Closed stomata mean the tree is conserving water but also slowing down its photosynthesis, since it isn’t taking in any carbon dioxide.
“Because leaves are a physical, light-absorbing object, they heat up just like asphalt would in the sun,” said Lily Klinek, a PhD student at UC Davis who was the lead author on the study.
“They’re heating up faster than the air around them,” she said. “And one way that they can cope with this is by opening their stomata and allowing water to transpire out of the leaf, which is kind of like the way that humans sweat. When water evaporates off our skin, it cools us down, and it’s the same for leaves. But they can only really do that if they have enough water to lose.”
Klinek and her colleagues studied coast redwoods in Mendocino County, near the southern part of their range, where the researchers used specialized instruments to measure whether or not individual leaves were photosynthesizing. During heat waves, they found, coast redwoods hit a point where they can’t cool down fast enough, and they just keep their stomata closed. While that saves water, it also means the tree isn’t taking in more carbon—which means it’s not “eating” or building up energy stores it can use to keep growing.
This may sound like a technicality of tree physiology. But it could have a big impact on these forests, creating a vicious cycle where trees don’t have enough carbon stored to replenish their leaves in the future, which means they won’t be able to photosynthesize as efficiently, which will starve them even further, repeating until trees eventually die. And while this sort of behavior has been observed in tropical trees, it’s the first time anyone has studied how coast redwoods respond to the same heat stress.
“The term people use is carbon starvation,” said Chris Still, a forest ecologist at Oregon State University who didn’t participate in the study. “Leaves can be expensive to build for a plant.”
Most of the redwoods in California and the Pacific Northwest nowadays are new-growth forests planted in the last couple of centuries. That means the trees are relatively hungry, like growing adolescents, compared to their old-growth cousins, so they need to suck in lots of carbon dioxide to grow taller.
Redwoods are also incredibly good at storing carbon. Thanks to their bulk and long lives, they store more carbon dioxide per acre than any other forest in the world. “Not only is it negative feedback on the climate system itself, with less carbon sequestration from these trees and forests, but the trees themselves are going to obviously not grow as big,” said Anthony Ambrose, a plant physiological ecologist and co-founder of the Ancient Forest Society. So even if the trees survive, they might not have as much space for fern and soil mats, which means less habitat for the creatures that live in them, and they may not grow as tall as they once used to, which could hurt them in another way.
A central threat to these trees, Klinek explained, is that in addition to the heat stress, they may also lose a crucial source of hydration and protection: Coast redwoods have an intricate relationship with the fogs of their native Northern California and the Pacific Northwest. The trees are so tall that their canopies reach high into fog layers, where they can sip water directly from the sky. The fog also shades the trees from the sun and helps coast redwoods create their own microclimate, which is why these forests are noticeably cooler than the areas adjacent to them. But warmer oceans and drier air are making fog more sporadic, which means the trees are missing a crucial source of relief from heat that is only getting more intense.
“It’s kind of a double whammy,” said Todd Dawson, a plant ecophysiologist at the University of California Berkeley, who also didn’t participate in the study. “They’re running out of water and also getting this heat stress,” he said. “They’re used to living in a very narrow temperature range of 8 to 27 degrees Celsius (about 46 to 80 degrees Fahrenheit). California, like everywhere, has been getting long periods of much warmer days than we’ve ever experienced, and now the fog, which is normally kind of like an air conditioner, has also declined between 30 and 40 percent.”
These temperature swings also impact the organisms living high up in the trees. “If they experience really excessive heat throughout the summer,” Ambrose said, “then the soil mats and ferns will probably dry out much faster. And then those salamanders and birds might not be able to live there. So we’ll see cascading effects through the whole ecosystem at that point.”
Klinek said, the trees seem to be doing okay after the heat passes; while the leaves she and her team looked at over their two-year study didn’t acclimate to the heat, they also didn’t lose their capacity to photosynthesize after the heat passed. While that’s a bit of hopeful news, it doesn’t reduce the urgency of the need to better understand the impact of climate change on these trees, and to reduce the warming itself.
“Right now the temperatures are coming back to normal in the fall and winter and letting the trees recover,” Klinek said. “But in five or 10 years, if temperatures are even hotter and heat waves are even more frequent, we don’t really know if there would be a recovery.”
For now, the salamanders and seabirds still have their homes high atop the coast redwoods. But we’re a part of the redwoods’ larger ecosystem too, even if we don’t live near them—they, like all trees, are key to keeping our planet hospitable. The trees Klinek studied have the potential to live for more than a thousand years. The question is if we’ll let them.

articles.title: Learning to use local AI is exciting, overwhelming, and frustrating
articles.text:
I’m embarking on a journey I’ve so far been hesitant to go on: actually using AI on the regular. Giving my most personal data to cloud services has been a major hold up for me, but it’s increasingly possible to run powerful models locally to see what they’re capable of. Is this tech so useful that it’s worth throwing gobs of money at a computer or a laptop with lots of overpriced RAM? I’ll try to help you find out. I’m not an AI expert, it’s going to be a journey for me, but maybe I can help you see if that journey is worth taking — and I’ll be posting my way through it.
Learning to use local AI is exciting, overwhelming, and frustrating
It’s like using cloud-based AI tools, but the privacy makes it more appealing.
Learning to use local AI is exciting, overwhelming, and frustrating
It’s like using cloud-based AI tools, but the privacy makes it more appealing.
A big part of Apple’s pitch for its new Mac desktops is how good they are for local AI, and there’s an entire line of new RTX Spark Windows machines landing imminently with up to 128GB of RAM aimed at using agentic AI. Local AI and agents are just, like, so hot right now. But, in all seriousness, the thought of having a little gofer living solely in the box on my desk that answers only to me and not overlords from OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, or Anthropic hits a bit different than trusting cloud services or subscribing to a chatbot. Don’t get me wrong, there’s still no way I’m gonna have it write for me, edit for me, or generate ugly fliers. But now, with some privacy on my side maybe I can finally think of useful busy work to “trust” it with.
So as part of my ongoing testing of the M5 Ultra Mac Studio, as well as experimenting on other Mac and Windows systems, I’ve installed some local LLMs and I’m beginning to tinker. Here’s how things are going.
I started by installing the open-source Hermes Agent on the Mac Studio. Hermes is a self-hosted AI agent desktop app that works on macOS, Windows, and Linux. It’s completely free to use if you stick to local LLMs. Since this M5 Ultra Mac Studio has 256GB of unified memory, I could run just about any model I want. This is how things quickly get overwhelming. There are more models out there than I can count, and some have specialized uses. Generally, models with many billions of parameters are able to do more than smaller ones with only a few billion. And since we don’t have to worry about paying for tokens when running a model locally, I figured I’d go big to start.
Using Hermes’ straightforward onboarding interface and model picker, I chose the Qwen 3.8 Flash Next model — a 125-billion parameter model that’s around 105GB in size. I also plan on spending some time with much smaller Qwen models on devices like an M6 Mac Mini, M5 MacBook Air, an Asus TUF Gaming A14 with AMD Strix Halo processor, and, eventually, RTX Spark. (Care to share what local models and hardware you use? You know where to leave your comments. 🫡)
It wasn’t long to get up and running with Hermes and Qwen, and even make them controllable via my phone by using a Telegram bot. But then, I was presented with my usual nemesis when it comes to using AI: the text box.
“What do I do with this thing?”
First up, to get things going, I followed some helpful YouTube advice and had Hermes make me a daily morning briefing — to just start small with a cron job and ensure things are working. It scans my email and calendar, tells me anything worth my immediate attention, and gives me a short weather report. It’s not all that useful, and you obviously don’t need a $12,000 computer to build it, but it’s something I can develop over time. The brief kept failing to generate at first, but then I eventually figured out that macOS couldn’t be asleep when the job fired up at 7:30am. Duh! It works like clockwork now, but I have to think of more info for it to pull for me to make the results more helpful.
A more useful task was reorganizing my Steam library. I have over 400 games on Steam, and I recently started categorizing them for when I want to play something new on a whim. Steam doesn’t categorize your games for you, so you instead have to do it manually, one-by-one. But here’s where an agentic lackey could fit right in. I asked, “Can you reorganize my Steam library?” Hermes could see most of my games by just viewing the already installed Steam client. It quickly came up with some organization options for me. I decided to have it organize my games by genre, but leave some of my own specialized categories(favorites, co-op titles, party games, games to play with my wife, etc.).
You have to give a local AI some permissions over your machine for it to take actions for you, and in the case of my game library I had to register a Steam web API key and give it to Hermes. Once it had that access, it only took a few minutes for it to churn through sorting all the games into categories. And the API key was easy to revoke right after, since I don’t need it further. The idea is for it to just do this heavy lifting for me once, and then I’ll file new games into the categories as I eventually buy them. It did a fine job overall, and now my Steam library is easily browsable.
Another simple thing I did was data analysis. I had Hermes take a look at financial records to crunch some numbers for me, and I also had it make me a spec comparison spreadsheet for a new laptop. These are small things, but they’re both tasks I cannot or will not trust with any cloud service — I don’t want to upload that sensitive data to the cloud, and in the case of a new laptop, that info was under embargo. Keeping them on my computer was the difference in me using this tool or not.
The bigger bit of automation I’m currently working on is a script to run a series of laptop benchmark tests. I run all our benchmarks manually, and tending to a laptop to run a dozen or so tests — three times over, to take the average — is incredibly time-consuming. I’d love to automate at least some of it. Even walking Hermes through all of the required procedures and getting it to spit out vibe coded Python scripts has been a bit of an endeavor, and it remains a work in progress. But I’m hoping to make some positive headway.
It’s still early days of me working with Hermes, and I’m hoping this is just the tip of the iceberg on the useful things I get it to do for me. But it’s also clear that even these powerful local models don’t make for a magical assistant that can do anything. Things still don’t always work as intended — my daily briefing already broke, multiple times.
I view Hermes and local AI as just a tool, a computer program to run on my computer. I don’t want a digital friend. I’m not saying “thank you” or “please,” or typing “sorry” when I change my mind on something. I’m remaining as stone-cold and indifferent when ordering it around as I am clicking a mouse around an operating system.
I hope to remain vigilant and cautious while I continue testing and learning with local AI. Let’s see where it takes me.

articles.title: Judge orders Trump admin to stop airing challenged government-funded ads immediately
articles.text:
A federal judge ordered the Trump administration Sunday night to immediately stop airing controversial government-funded ads that have been called propaganda and criticized as being aimed at influencing the upcoming midterm election.
The ads were being funded by a $20 million contract from the Department of Homeland Security.
The coalition of plaintiffs that sued to block continued airing of the ads in U.S. District Court in Manhattan include the advocacy group Common Cause and the Service Employees International Union Local 32BJ, which is headquartered in New York City.
"The Court finds that (1) the present motion is not moot, (2) there is standing to proceed, and (3) the moving Plaintiffs have demonstrated that they are likely to succeed on the merits, will suffer irreparable harm in the absence of an injunction, the balance of the equities tips in their favor, and an injunction serves the public interest," Judge Jennifer Rochon wrote in her order.
The coalition, in a statement, said, "We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda."
"There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda," the coalition said, referring to President Donald Trump. "As this case moves forward and voters make their voices heard in this election, we will work to ensure the rule of law continues to be upheld, protecting the rights of voters and our democracy."
This is developing news. Check back for updates.

articles.title: Plenty is working against this market. Here's why I'm staying invested anyway
articles.text: We all know I am not allowed to own individual stocks. But I am permitted to own index funds, and I have methodically invested a decent chunk of my earnings each month into an S & P 500 index fund. Sometimes I want to balk so badly that it is palpable. Nothing is happening that I think should happen, so maybe I skip contributing for a month. Just keep it in cash. That's in sync with what we are doing in the Investing Club where we have a ton of cash. Sure, there are always individual stocks I want to own; you see in the charitable trust. But the fact is, I don't have a strong case for owning stocks at the moment. We are heading into an earnings season where expectations, at last, seem too high. It isn't like the off-cycle earnings reports we have seen lately have been dazzling. We don't get much encouragement from the world's stories. Why aren't the Saudis fighting back aftr attacks by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen.? Why are we siding with the Russians just to get some diesel fuel? I can't imagine how many presidents are rolling over in their graves on that one. There is no end in sight to the war in Iran. And the narrative that Iran will just collapse because there is no new money coming in from oil is antithetical to this extreme regime, which prides itself on a spartan life. The possibility that these faceless leaders might make a deal to prevent being overthrown was dead when the country decided to murder its dissenters before the war began. Europe has crept back on the scene in a real negative way, this time with France on the hot seat. The country is dealing with a growing debt crisis, a budget deadlock, and widespread protests. I don't think that France will precipitate a crisis because the EU — post the 2011 European sovereign debt crisis — has methods to deal with the wayward. The real problem is that there are plenty of people who are probably betting wrong (a la Situational Awareness ) on France, and maybe on Japan for that matter. There's going to be no end to the negative international headlines. Of course, the worst of all is the increasingly hostile attitude toward the data center and the companies spending on them. I look at the world's largest company, Nvidia, as the bellwether, and there is no doubt its stock is stuck. The AI chipmaker can't get rid of the circular financing view and the concerns that there will be fewer clients because of the data center bans. Rather than cloture, the midterm elections may bring affirmation of a rolling building ban. Given that the only real oomph in the entire economy is coming from the data center buildout, it is difficult to see where the market's energy is going to come from. After all, the Federal Reserve is hellbent on getting inflation to 2%, and its moves are raising the long end of the yield curve — although most just say that's caused by inflation or supply. We seem to be headed inexorably to 6% and change yield on the 30-year Treasury bond, at which time we are going to lose whatever is left of the housing market. But that got me to thinking something. If you are investing for the next month or two, I can see how you might want to skip October. I know that September is historically the worst month, and it is only anecdotally a terrible month; we have 1929 and 1987 crashes to thank for what is otherwise a pretty successful time in the market. It only feels like a crash because it always feels like a crash right now for one reason or another. So what did I do? The money is meant to be invested for the long term. I can't and don't trade it. My hope is that Fed Chief Kevin Warsh actually does take inflation down to 2%, and that interest rates will go so high that it pressures lawmakers in Washington to rein in the federal deficit by cutting some spending here and there and increasing taxes to stop the lunacy of this deficit. It hasn't happened yet. And it won't happen in October if I decided to skip my October contribution. But if I truly believe that Warsh is a man of his word, that he will not fold under a president that wants rates cut, then I have to keep putting money to work in the market. Plus, like staying in shape, investing has to be done regularly or else. I genuinely think that, after all of these years of automatic contributions, if I skip one, there will be many others that are skipped. I look back and wonder what would have happened to my savings if I had decided to look at that day's headlines and decide I am crazy to put money into this market. The answer? I probably wouldn't have as much money saved for retirement. So I close my eyes to the short term. I accept that I have to buy a lot of stocks in the S & P 500 that I hate — unlike you Club members that can also own individual stocks. I invest knowing that, as crazy as it has been, I have made a lot of money with stocks. And as crazy as it might be, I believe I can do so again.
